title: HM Revenue & Customs reports about £4.6 billion of additional tax yield in 2024–25 from cases flagged by its Connect data-matching system
summary: HM Revenue & Customs estimates that cases flagged by its Connect data-matching system yielded about £4.6 billion of additional tax in 2024–25.
account: HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) launched Connect in 2010–11. Its annual report calls Connect an information technology system that joins a billion pieces of data across its tax regimes to help identify fraud. In February 2015 the National Audit Office called Connect a good illustration of HMRC's ability to use new technology. It cited HMRC's figures of about £80 million invested since 2008 and £3 billion of extra revenue. Drawing on HMRC's annual report, it also said that Connect let HMRC cut its Risk and Intelligence staff by 40% while it collected more compliance revenue. The Comptroller and Auditor General's report in HMRC's 2024–25 accounts records that HMRC used TRUCE (Transaction Risking Upstream in a Connect Environment). It served to identify and stop value-added tax and income-tax repayments that may require investigation. A system called IDRS replaced it from August 2023. The official sources describe Connect's methods as data analytics and risk rules, and none of them calls Connect AI. In a freedom-of-information response reported by Pinsent Masons on 8 October 2025, HMRC said that Connect cases generated an average £3.4 billion of additional annual yield, about £4.6 billion in 2024–25, with around 4,300 staff using the system. The Comptroller and Auditor General notes that compliance yield, the measure behind the £4.6 billion, is HMRC's own estimate of the revenue that it considers it generated and the losses that it prevented. HMRC's annual report for 2025–26, ordered printed on 9 July 2026, credits AI and advanced analytics with the protection and recovery of £10 billion in tax in 2025–26 and does not name Connect.
purpose: Match and analyze data from many sources to identify tax non-compliance and risky repayment claims
system: HMRC Connect (data-matching and risk analytics) and TRUCE (Transaction Risking Upstream in a Connect Environment)
domain: Tax administration: compliance and fraud detection
taxonomy_note: Tax yield is read as the authority's revenue; Trustible's description is written for product sales.

ratings.reason: The sources report an aggregate yield and name no person who gained from it.

HMRC reports about £4.6 billion of extra yield from Connect cases in 2024–25. In a 2015 case study that draws on HMRC's own annual report, the National Audit Office says that Connect let HMRC cut its Risk and Intelligence staff by 40% while it collected more compliance revenue. Both are measurable gains in HMRC's results. The figures are HMRC's own estimates, and the Comptroller and Auditor General describes compliance yield as such.
No source traces the extra revenue to an effect on the public, such as funded services or a smaller tax gap.

ai_role.statement: Yield attribution to Connect comes from HMRC's FOI response as reported by Pinsent Masons. No independent evaluation apportions yield between the system and caseworkers. The NAO's audit report describes TRUCE/IDRS as automated risk-assessment of repayment claims whose controls it reviewed, without quantifying stopped repayments. The cited sources describe the system as data analytics and risk rules rather than machine learning.

fields.summary: HM Revenue & Customs estimates that cases flagged by its Connect data-matching system yielded about £4.6 billion of additional tax in 2024–25.
fields.account: HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) launched Connect in 2010–11. Its annual report calls Connect an information technology system that joins a billion pieces of data across its tax regimes to help identify fraud. In February 2015 the National Audit Office called Connect a good illustration of HMRC's ability to use new technology. It cited HMRC's figures of about £80 million invested since 2008 and £3 billion of extra revenue. Drawing on HMRC's annual report, it also said that Connect let HMRC cut its Risk and Intelligence staff by 40% while it collected more compliance revenue. The Comptroller and Auditor General's report in HMRC's 2024–25 accounts records that HMRC used TRUCE (Transaction Risking Upstream in a Connect Environment). It served to identify and stop value-added tax and income-tax repayments that may require investigation. A system called IDRS replaced it from August 2023. The official sources describe Connect's methods as data analytics and risk rules, and none of them calls Connect AI. In a freedom-of-information response reported by Pinsent Masons on 8 October 2025, HMRC said that Connect cases generated an average £3.4 billion of additional annual yield, about £4.6 billion in 2024–25, with around 4,300 staff using the system. The Comptroller and Auditor General notes that compliance yield, the measure behind the £4.6 billion, is HMRC's own estimate of the revenue that it considers it generated and the losses that it prevented. HMRC's annual report for 2025–26, ordered printed on 9 July 2026, credits AI and advanced analytics with the protection and recovery of £10 billion in tax in 2025–26 and does not name Connect.
